doc.title: Geometric Deep Learning Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges

proposal.title: A Geometric Blueprint for Deep Learning
proposal.gist: A single geometric blueprint—symmetry, scale separation, equivariance—explains and unifies most deep learning architectures.
proposal.question: Deep learning architectures — why do so many unrelated-looking networks share the same hidden structure? (a unifying blueprint)

children.title: Title Page and Contents
children.gist: The paper's title, authors, affiliations, and table of contents.

children.title: Preface and Notation
children.gist: Following Felix Klein's Erlangen Programme, which unified geometries by their symmetry groups, the authors propose classifying deep learning architectures the same way.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning — what historical precedent justifies unifying neural network architectures by symmetry? (a historical analogy)

children.title: Preface
children.gist: Klein's Erlangen Programme redefined geometry as the study of invariants under symmetry groups, revealing how different classical geometries relate through group inclusion, a mindset the authors now apply to deep learning.

children.title: Notation
children.gist: A glossary of the mathematical symbols used throughout the text.

children.title: Deep Learning Needs Geometry
children.gist: Deep learning's success rests on representation learning and gradient descent exploiting the low-dimensional, symmetric structure of real-world data, motivating a geometric unification of its architectures.
children.question: Deep learning's success — why do neural networks work despite the curse of dimensionality? (a unifying geometric view)

children.title: The Deep Learning Revolution
children.gist: Deep learning's rapid success across vision, games, and biology comes from combining hierarchical feature learning with gradient descent, exploiting the fact that real tasks have low-dimensional physical structure, not pure scale.

children.title: Scope and Limitations
children.gist: The authors restrict their focus to representation-learning architectures and the symmetries they exploit, deliberately excluding optimization tricks and other pipelines, while studying select architectures deeply rather than exhaustively.

children.title: Learning in High Dimensions
children.gist: Generic high-dimensional function estimation is intractable, so learning needs inductive biases, and physically structured data offers an escape from this curse.
children.question: High-dimensional learning — why does the curse of dimensionality make generic estimation hopeless, and what helps? (two complexity results)

children.title: Supervised Learning Setup
children.gist: Supervised learning assumes labels come from an unknown function over a high-dimensional space, judges performance by expected loss on new samples, and therefore needs the right notion of regularity to succeed.

children.title: Inductive Bias via Function Regularity
children.gist: Neural networks can universally approximate almost any function, but genuine generalization instead comes from a complexity measure favoring simpler solutions, as seen in weight decay, splines, and implicit optimization bias.

children.title: The Curse of Dimensionality
children.gist: Classic regularity classes like Lipschitz or Sobolev functions require exponentially many samples as dimension grows, and even sparsity-promoting networks only escape this curse under unrealistic assumptions about the target function.

children.title: Geometric Priors
children.gist: Symmetry, approximate invariance under deformation, and scale separation together define the geometric priors that let a general deep learning blueprint be derived from first principles.
children.question: Geometric priors — what principles let neural networks escape the limits of high-dimensional learning? (three principles)

children.title: Priors from the Domain
children.gist: Physically structured data admits two rescue principles against the curse of dimensionality, symmetry and scale separation, both naturally expressed through signals defined over some underlying geometric domain.

children.title: Symmetries, Representations, and Invariance
children.gist: Symmetries of a domain form a group, and functions built on it can be invariant or equivariant to that group, with CNNs combining both via convolution followed by pooling.

children.title: Isomorphisms and Automorphisms
children.gist: A domain can carry several levels of structure, from bare sets to metrics to manifolds, each with its own symmetry group, so adding structure always shrinks the group of allowed transformations.

children.title: Deformation Stability
children.gist: Because real-world transformations are rarely exact symmetries, functions should instead be stable to small deformations of signals or of the domain itself, generalizing strict invariance into an approximate, measurable notion.

children.title: Scale Separation
children.gist: Multiscale wavelet decompositions localize signals in both space and frequency, unlike the Fourier transform, remaining stable under small deformations and motivating a scale-separation prior that progressively coarsens the domain.

children.title: The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: Combining local equivariant maps, nonlinearities, coarsening operators, and global invariant pooling yields a universal blueprint from which architectures like CNNs and graph neural networks can all be derived.
children.sourceHeading: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning

children.title: Geometric Domains: the 5 Gs
children.gist: Grids, graphs, groups, manifolds, and gauges are the five domains whose symmetries determine how convolution-like operations must be built on them.
children.question: The 5 Gs — how does each geometric domain's symmetry shape its natural notion of convolution? (five domains surveyed)

children.title: Introducing the 5 Gs
children.gist: The text organizes geometric domains into five families, grids, groups, graphs, geodesics, and gauges, chosen to highlight key concepts rather than strict generality, since grids are themselves special graphs.

children.title: Graphs and Sets
children.gist: Graphs model relations between unordered nodes, so functions on them must be permutation invariant or equivariant, built by locally aggregating each node's neighborhood features in an order-independent way.

children.title: Groups and Homogeneous Spaces
children.gist: Convolution and the Fourier transform generalize to any group acting transitively on a domain, illustrated by cyclic shifts and spherical rotations, though integrating over very large groups becomes impractical.

children.title: Geodesics and Manifolds
children.gist: Manifolds lack global symmetry but carry intrinsic structure, metrics, geodesics, and a Laplacian, letting convolution be defined spectrally or spatially while remaining invariant to isometric deformations.

children.title: Gauges and Bundles
children.gist: Features on manifolds are expressed relative to an arbitrary local frame or gauge, so network functions built on them must be equivariant to gauge transformations, a symmetry distinct from the domain's own.

children.title: Geometric Graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Triangular meshes discretize manifolds with their own intrinsic metrics and Laplacians, letting spectral and spatial convolutions be built via cotangent weights and functional maps that are stable to remeshing.

children.title: Geometric Deep Learning Models
children.gist: CNNs, group-equivariant networks, graph neural networks, mesh networks, and recurrent networks all instantiate the same blueprint of equivariant layers, pooling, and invariant readout.
children.question: Deep learning architectures — how do CNNs, GNNs, mesh networks and RNNs all realize the same geometric blueprint? (eight architecture families)

children.title: From Blueprint to Architectures
children.gist: Having built the general blueprint, the text now shows how concrete architectures, CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, mesh networks, and RNNs, all instantiate it for their particular domain and symmetry group.

children.title: Convolutional Neural Networks
children.gist: Convolutional networks implement local translation-equivariant linear filters followed by nonlinearity and pooling across scales, with residual connections and normalization enabling very deep, trainable architectures.

children.title: Group-equivariant CNNs
children.gist: Generalizing translation to richer groups like discrete rotations or DNA's reverse-complement symmetry, group convolutions can be implemented efficiently by first transforming filters and then convolving as in ordinary CNNs.

children.title: Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Nearly all GNN layers reduce to one of three flavours, fixed-weight convolutional aggregation, attention-weighted aggregation, or full message passing, each strictly more expressive but harder to scale than the last.

children.title: Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference
children.gist: Choosing an empty, complete, or learned edge set over unordered nodes yields Deep Sets, Transformers' self-attention, or latent graph inference respectively, all as special cases of graph neural networks.
children.sourceHeading: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference

children.title: Equivariant Message Passing Networks
children.gist: For molecular graphs with spatial coordinates, equivariant message passing keeps features invariant and coordinates equivariant to rotations and translations by depending only on pairwise distances between connected nodes.

children.title: Intrinsic Mesh CNNs
children.gist: Mesh CNNs approximate convolution via geodesic patches expressed in local tangent coordinates, resolving the ambiguity of gauge choice through isotropic filters, angular pooling, fixed gauges, or gauge-equivariant filters.

children.title: Recurrent Neural Networks
children.gist: Recurrent networks summarize sequential inputs step by step and can be shown to be equivariant to shifts under suitable padding and initial conditions, though simple RNNs suffer badly from vanishing gradients.

children.title: Long Short-Term Memory Networks
children.gist: Gated RNNs like the LSTM use learnable input, forget, and output gates to control memory retention, which can be shown to make them invariant to a wide class of time-warping transformations.

children.title: Problems and Applications
children.gist: Geometric Deep Learning already drives real advances in drug discovery, protein design, recommendation, traffic prediction, vision, games, language, medicine, and physics.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning in practice — which real-world domains has it already transformed? (nine application areas)

children.title: Chemistry and Drug Design
children.gist: Graph neural networks screen vast spaces of candidate molecules for useful properties, as shown when one discovered Halicin, a repurposed diabetes drug later found to be a potent antibiotic.

children.title: Protein Biology
children.gist: Representing proteins as contact graphs or molecular surface meshes lets graph and mesh neural networks predict folding-related function and even design novel proteins that bind cancer-relevant targets.

children.title: Recommender Systems and Social Networks
children.gist: Large-scale graph neural networks power production recommender systems like Pinterest's PinSage and detect misinformation by modeling how news items propagate through user-sharing networks on social media.

children.title: Traffic Forecasting
children.gist: Modeling road networks as graphs lets graph neural networks predict estimated arrival times, now deployed at scale within Google Maps and Baidu Maps for millions of daily travelers.

children.title: Object Recognition
children.gist: Convolutional networks trained on ImageNet, from AlexNet through ResNets, surpassed human-level image classification, while related translation-equivariant models advanced object detection and semantic segmentation.

children.title: Game Playing
children.gist: Convolutional networks extracting features from grid-based game states powered DeepMind's AlphaGo and its successors, eventually reaching superhuman performance across Go, Chess, Shogi, and Atari games.

children.title: Text and Speech Synthesis
children.gist: One-dimensional convolutional and Transformer architectures, exploiting grid-like structure in text and audio, now generate human-like speech and text, powering systems like WaveNet, BERT, and GPT-3.

children.title: Healthcare
children.gist: Grid-based CNNs, mesh networks for organ surfaces, and graph networks for brain connectivity or patient similarity are increasingly used across diagnosis, prognosis, and medical image analysis tasks.

children.title: Particle Physics, Astrophysics, and Virtual Reality
children.gist: Graph and spherical neural networks model particle jets, neutrino detectors, and cosmic microwave background radiation, while mesh networks drive 3D body and hand reconstruction for virtual reality.

children.title: Historic Perspective
children.gist: Symmetry has organized mathematics and physics since Klein and Noether, and graph neural networks' own history shows convergent rediscovery across chemistry, AI, and signal processing.
children.question: Symmetry's history — how did today's geometric deep learning methods emerge from decades of separate traditions? (a historical survey)

children.title: Symmetry in Mathematics and Physics
children.gist: Symmetry has organized mathematics and physics since antiquity, formalized through group theory, Noether's theorem linking symmetry to conservation laws, and gauge invariance underlying the Standard Model of particle physics.

children.title: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
children.gist: Early pattern recognition work on equivariant feature detectors and the Neocognitron's shift-invariant hierarchical design, inspired by the visual cortex, directly anticipated modern convolutional neural networks.
children.sourceHeading: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning

children.title: Origins of Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Graph neural networks arose independently from 1990s structure-processing networks, computational chemistry's molecular graph models, and unsupervised random-walk node embeddings, later converging with probabilistic graphical model message passing.

children.title: The Weisfeiler-Lehman Formalism
children.gist: Graph neural networks are provably no more powerful than the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test, motivating injective aggregation functions and higher-order architectures that exceed this expressive limit.

children.title: Signal Processing and Harmonic Analysis
children.gist: Harmonic analysis traditions from computational neuroscience and computer graphics, including scattering transforms and graph or mesh spectral methods, independently developed the mathematical tools now underlying spectral graph networks.

children.title: Algorithmic Reasoning
children.gist: Neural networks can be designed to mimic algorithms' control flow and preserve their invariants, with graph neural networks shown to align naturally with dynamic programming and generalize to unseen input sizes.

children.title: Naming Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: The term Geometric Deep Learning originated in 2015, naming a field whose '5G' domains, grids, graphs, groups, geodesics, and gauges, give this text its organizing structure.
